From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
To: Samir Gupta <samir.gupta@acmecorp.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: ACME discovery recap + sample schema — technical details

Hi Samir / Marissa —

Thanks for the detailed notes + schema. Below are concise answers and recommended patterns you can adopt quickly. Happy to jump on a 20m call to walk through examples.

1) Chat vs Completions (tokenization/truncation)
- Under the hood tokenization is model-dependent (same tokenizer for both endpoints for a given model family). Chat vs completions is an API surface difference: chat wraps messages (role/content) but tokens are counted on the concatenated serialized message payload.
- Practically: you will not see different truncation semantics solely because you use chat vs completions. Truncation happens when the total token count (prompt + response) exceeds model max context; Redwood enforces per-request limits and will return a 413-style error if prompt is too large unless you enable automatic prefix trimming.

2) max_tokens accounting & stop sequences
- max_tokens controls the server-side cap on generated tokens. Redwood counts generated tokens (post-start) toward max_tokens; stop sequences are checked during generation and do not consume extra budget beyond the tokens the model emits. If a stop sequence triggers mid-token the behavior depends on tokenizer alignment: we post-process to ensure stop sequences are respected and trim trailing partial tokens if needed.
- For streaming: tokens are yielded as they are produced. The max_tokens cap still applies server-side; when the model reaches the cap or emits a stop sequence, the stream ends. From a client perspective you get partial chunks until the final stop/end-of-stream event.

3) Guaranteeing parseable JSON (structured output)
- Best practice: use function/tool calling where the model returns a structured object that the runtime validates against the declared schema. This is the most robust approach for guaranteed typed outputs.
- If you prefer free-text JSON, combine stop sequences with strict system prompts and runtime schema validation: run the model output through a JSON linter and, on parse errors, either re-call with the previous context or fall back to a safer path.
- Redwood SDKs provide a validate_response(schema, output) helper and automatic retries for parse failures (configurable). Example pattern:
  1) Declare function with JSON schema (fields: action, type, payload).
  2) Call model with function-calling enabled.
  3) On return, runtime asserts schema; if it fails, SDK can retry with higher temperature=0 and a deterministic prompt to correct format.

4) Streaming semantics
- Streaming returns incremental token deltas. For chat-style streams we emit role/content deltas as they arrive (common pattern: {role: "assistant", delta: "text chunk"}). The final event includes metadata (finish_reason: "stop" | "max_tokens").
- Important: do not rely on complete JSON until the finish event; for large structured outputs prefer function-calling (final object arrives as a single coherent payload).

5) Embeddings vs Reranker tradeoffs
- Embedding-only retrieval (ANN search + cosine score) is fast and cheap; good initial recall.
- Reranker (a small instruct-tuned model or cross-encoder) is more expensive but improves precision for top-K results and reorders by relevance taking context into account. Recommendation: use embeddings for candidate generation (K=50) + lightweight reranker (K=10) for production if precision matters (agents with few-turn SLOs).

6) Auth & SDK patterns
- Options: API keys (simple), OAuth2 (customer-facing integrations), mutual TLS (mTLS) for on-prem connectors. For ACME, given regulatory constraints, mTLS for private connectors + API keys for hosted calls is a common pattern.
- SDKs: we ship JS/Python snippets that handle chunked streaming, resume, and validate_response(schema). Example pseudo-code (JS):

  const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.RW_API_KEY });
  const fn = { name: 'perform_action', schema: { type: 'object', properties: { action: {type:'string'}, payload: {type:'object'}}, required:['action'] } };
  const res = await client.chat.call({ messages, functions:[fn], function_call: 'auto', stream: true });
  // SDK will emit chunks; subscribe to 'finish' event to get final structured payload and run validate_response(fn.schema, payload)

Operational tips:
- For strict latency SLOs, pin region and choose a model/quant profile that meets median latency on your benchmark.
- Use prefix/KV cache when you have many repeated system instructions to reduce tokens and latency.

Happy to join a follow-up with your infra team — tell me some times next week and I’ll block.
